t: The rules framed by the Central Government to give effect to the MV Act 1988 are the:
o: Indian Motor Tariff Rules, 2002
Motor Vehicles (Third Party) Rules, 1988
Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989
Road Transport Rules, 1990
e: The Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989, along with State rules and the Rules of the Road Regulations, constitute the body of law regulating road transport.

t: Section 146 prohibits the use of a motor vehicle in a public place without an Act policy by any person:
o: Except the registered owner
Except as a passenger
Except Government employees
Except holders of a learner's licence
e: Section 146(1): no person shall use, except as a passenger, or cause or allow any other person to use, a motor vehicle in a public place unless a policy complying with Chapter XI is in force.

t: Under the amended Act, which statutory provision on 'pay and recover' by the insurer was deleted?
o: Section 149(4) of the pre-amendment Act
Section 170
Section 166(4)
Section 147(5)
e: The pay-and-recover provision in old s.149(4) was deleted in 2019; however the Supreme Court continues to apply the pay-and-recover principle (K. Nagendra, 2025) in cases of technical breach.

t: Under the detailed accident report scheme, the victims must furnish their particulars in Forms VI-A and VI-B to the Investigating Officer within:
o: 90 days
10 days
30 days
60 days
e: Victim forms within 60 days; driver and owner forms within 30 days; DAR within 90 days.

t: Which term used under the old hit-and-run provisions was dropped by the 2019 amendment?
o: Motor Vehicle Accident Fund
Solatium Fund
Good Samaritan
Claims Tribunal
e: The amended s.161 makes no mention of the Solatium Fund; hit-and-run compensation is now paid from the Hit and Run Compensation Fund under the Motor Vehicle Accident Fund (s.164B).

t: Section 162 of the amended MV Act casts an obligation on:
o: State Governments to pay all medical bills of victims
Vehicle owners to deposit ₹1.5 lakh with the hospital
Hospitals to treat all accident victims free of cost permanently
General insurers in India to provide for treatment of road accident victims, including during the golden hour, under schemes made under the Act
e: Section 162(1) requires insurers carrying on general insurance business to provide for treatment of road accident victims including during the golden hour, and s.162(2) requires the Central Government to make a cashless treatment scheme.

t: 'Community service' as inserted by Section 2(4A) of the amended Act means:
o: Unpaid work which a person is required to perform as punishment for an offence under the Act
Voluntary service by Good Samaritans at accident sites
Paid work by convicts in road construction
Service by insurers in settling claims at Lok Adalats
e: Section 2(4A) defines community service as unpaid work ordered as punishment for an offence under the MV Act, introduced as an alternative penalty.

t: A tractor attached with a trailer carrying goods is treated under the MV Act as:
o: A light motor vehicle only
An adapted vehicle
A private service vehicle
A goods vehicle
e: A tractor by itself carries no load except the driver and propulsion equipment; when a trailer with goods is attached, the combination is deemed a goods vehicle.

t: 'Unladen weight' of a vehicle means:
o: The weight of the chassis alone
The weight of the vehicle with full fuel and passengers
The weight of the vehicle including all equipment ordinarily used with it when working, excluding the weight of the driver or attendant
The weight of the vehicle plus the permissible load certified by the registering authority
e: ULW excludes the driver/attendant and includes equipment ordinarily used; where alternative bodies are used, the heaviest body counts. GVW is vehicle plus permissible load.

t: Which Chapter of the MV Act, dealing with 'Liability without fault in certain cases' (Sections 140–144), was deleted by the 2019 amendment?
o: Chapter XII
Chapter IX
Chapter X
Chapter XI
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). Chapter X (Sections 140–144) on no-fault interim liability was omitted; no-fault compensation is now a fixed, final payment under the new Section 164 in Chapter XI.

t: Under Section 81, a permit (other than a temporary permit) is effective from the date of issue or renewal for:
o: Ten years
One year
Three years
Five years
e: Section 81 fixes a five-year validity for permits; s.87 temporary permits are limited to four months.

t: The offence of theft of a motor vehicle (old Section 379 IPC) falls under which section of BNS 2023?
o: Section 281
Section 106
Section 303
Section 379
e: Section 379 IPC → Section 303 BNS 2023.

t: In Sarla Verma, Step 1 of the computation ('ascertaining the multiplicand') involves:
o: Selecting the multiplier from the age table
Determining the annual income and deducting the amount the deceased would have spent on personal and living expenses
Adding the conventional heads
Multiplying the annual income by the number of dependants
e: Step 1 – multiplicand (annual income less personal expenses = contribution to dependants); Step 2 – multiplier by age; Step 3 – multiplicand × multiplier = loss of dependency.

t: The Supreme Court decision in K. Nagendra (October 2025) reaffirmed which principle in motor third party claims?
o: Lok Adalat awards are appealable
Pay and recover – the insurer first pays the third party victim even where the owner committed a technical breach, then recovers from the owner
Fixed compensation under Section 164 is interim
Transport endorsement is mandatory for all LMVs
e: Despite deletion of statutory s.149(4), the Court continues to direct insurers to pay the victim and recover from the owner where the breach is technical.

t: For a deceased aged 45 in a permanent job, the addition for future prospects is:
e: Permanent job: 50% (below 40), 30% (40–50), 15% (above 50). Self-employed/fixed salary: 40%, 25%, 10%.

t: Where the deceased was married and had two or three dependants, the deduction towards personal expenses is:
e: Married: 2–3 dependants → 1/3; 4–6 → 1/4; more than 6 → 1/5. Bachelor: 1/2 (parents only) or 1/3 (with siblings).

t: As per the multiplier table approved in Pranay Sethi, the multiplier applicable where the deceased was aged 41 to 45 years is:
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). The Sarla Verma table starts at 18 for ages 15–25 and reduces by one per five-year band: 17 (26–30), 16 (31–35), 15 (36–40), 14 (41–45), 13 (46–50), then 11, 9, 7 and 5.

t: 'Filial consortium' refers to:
o: The right of parents to compensation on the accidental death of their child
The right of a spouse to compensation on the death of the partner
Compensation for loss of estate
The right of children on the premature death of a parent
e: Spousal consortium – spouse; parental consortium – children on the death of a parent; filial consortium – parents on the death of a child (Magma v. Nanu Ram, 2018).

t: Per the trainers' limitation table, an appeal in an MCOP (motor claims) case must be filed within:
o: 6 months from the award
30 days from the award
90 days from the date of receipt of the award
60 days from the award
e: MCOP appeal – 90 days (s.173); EC Act appeal – 60 days; consumer appeal – 30 days.

t: The scientific test primarily used by the police to detect drunken driving under Section 185 is:
o: Breath analyser test
Reflex test
Vision test
Urine test
e: Section 185 refers to detection by a breath analyser (or other prescribed test) of alcohol exceeding 30 mg per 100 ml of blood.

t: Under the amended Section 194, overloading a goods vehicle attracts a minimum fine of:
o: ₹20,000 plus ₹2,000 per tonne of excess load
₹2,000 plus ₹1,000 per tonne
₹5,000 flat
e: Section 194(1): ₹20,000 plus ₹2,000 per excess tonne and the load must be off-loaded; s.194A imposes ₹200 per excess passenger.

t: Which of the following claims would an insurer be justified in declining as falling outside the Act policy?
o: Injury to a person riding on the trolley of a tractor-trailer carrying sand
Injury to the conductor of the insured bus in the accident
Damage to a Government electricity pole by the insured bus
Death of a pedestrian hit by the insured goods truck
e: Unauthorised persons in a goods vehicle and persons travelling on tractors/trailers are not third parties; pedestrians, Government property and co-workers on a transport vehicle are covered.

t: In a death claim at a Lok Adalat, the computed loss of dependency is ₹18,90,000 and conventional heads ₹2,28,000. The claimant's counsel demands interest of ₹2,65,000 in addition. The insurer should:
o: Refuse settlement and insist on trial
Pay the full ₹23,83,000 including interest
Settle for up to ₹21,18,000, since interest is not part of a consent settlement at Lok Adalat
Pay only ₹5,00,000 under Section 164
e: The computed amount under the judgements is the maximum for a Lok Adalat compromise; interest under s.171 and costs attach only to a contested award.

t: Which statement about the designated officer's offer under Section 149 is correct?
o: If the claimant rejects the offer, the Tribunal fixes a date of hearing to adjudicate the claim on merits
A rejected offer automatically becomes the award
The offer, once made, cannot be lower than ₹5 lakh
A rejected offer binds the claimant to arbitration
e: Section 149(3)(b): on rejection of the offer, the Tribunal fixes a hearing date and adjudicates the claim on merits.

t: An insurer repudiates a TP claim because the driver's licence was for 'motorcycle with gear' only and he was driving a car. Under Section 150(2) this is:
o: Not a defence, as any licence suffices under the MV Act
A defence only if the accident was due to drunken driving
A valid defence – driving by a person not duly licensed for that class of vehicle
A defence only if the car was a transport vehicle
e: Section 150(2)(a)(ii) covers driving by a person not duly licensed; a licence for a different class does not make the driver duly licensed for the vehicle driven. Courts may still order pay-and-recover.

t: A policy was issued but the proposal form concealed that the vehicle was earlier declared a total loss and rebuilt. After a TP accident, the insurer's defence under Section 150(2)(b) requires it to prove:
o: That the driver was negligent
That the premium was paid late
Merely that some information was incomplete
Non-disclosure of a material fact or a false representation in some material particular that renders the policy void
e: The policy must be shown to be void for non-disclosure of a material fact or material misrepresentation; immaterial omissions do not suffice.

t: A pedestrian is injured by an unidentified vehicle and treated cashlessly at a designated hospital for ₹60,000 under the 2025 Scheme. The hospital's claim for this treatment is reimbursed from:
o: The Hit and Run Compensation Fund / uninsured and hit-and-run account of the Motor Vehicle Accident Fund
The Account for Insured Vehicles
The pedestrian's own health insurer
The State Road Safety Council's budget
e: Hospitals' cashless treatment claims for hit-and-run and uninsured-vehicle victims are met from the uninsured/hit-and-run account and the Hit and Run Compensation Fund, administered by GIC.

t: The offence of rash or negligent driving on a public way, formerly Section 279 IPC, is now covered by:
o: Section 106 BNS
Section 303 BNS
Section 281 BNS
Section 125 BNS
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). Section 279 IPC maps to Section 281 BNS 2023. Section 106 is causing death by negligence, Section 125 is endangering life or personal safety, and Section 303 is theft.

t: In a Section 164 claim for death, the insurer argues the deceased was crossing the road negligently and seeks a 50% reduction. The Tribunal should:
o: Dismiss the claim for contributory negligence
Direct the claimant to file under Section 166
Reduce the compensation to ₹2,50,000
Reject the argument – s.164 compensation is payable without regard to wrongful act or neglect of any party, and the amount is fixed
e: Section 164 liability is no-fault: the claimant need not prove negligence and the fixed amount is not reduced for the victim's negligence; contributory negligence applies to s.166 fault-based claims.

t: An insurer wishes to deny liability in a Section 166 claim on the ground that the claimant has not filed the police charge sheet. The Tribunal is likely to:
o: Transfer the case to the criminal court
Adjourn sine die till the criminal trial concludes
Proceed with a summary inquiry using the accident information report/DAR under Section 159 and other evidence, since it has civil-court powers and is not bound by the criminal case
Dismiss the claim for want of charge sheet
e: Section 159 requires the police to furnish the accident information report to the Tribunal; the Tribunal (s.169) follows a summary procedure and decides negligence on preponderance of probability.

t: A Tribunal awards 7.5% simple interest from the date of the accident, which is eight months before the petition was filed. The insurer appeals on the interest start date. Under Section 171:
o: Interest must run from the date of deposit
Interest must run only from the date of the award
Interest cannot run from a date earlier than the date of making the claim, so the award is incorrect on this point
Interest from the accident date is mandatory
e: Section 171 permits simple interest from such date 'not earlier than the date of making the claim' as the Tribunal specifies.

t: A claimant awarded ₹4 lakh wants ₹12 lakh and files an appeal on the 100th day after the award without any deposit. Position:
o: The appeal is barred because the claimant cannot appeal
The appeal is beyond the 90-day limit (condonation needed on sufficient cause); the deposit requirement applies only to the person liable to pay the award
The appeal requires a deposit of ₹25,000 by the claimant
The appeal is in time and maintainable without deposit
e: Section 173: appeal within 90 days, with a proviso allowing condonation for sufficient cause; the deposit of ₹25,000/50% applies to the person required to pay the award.

t: Which of the following statements regarding permits is correct?
o: A permit, once issued, can never be transferred to another vehicle
A permit is required for every vehicle including private cars
A stage carriage can never be used as a contract carriage
A goods carriage permit allows the vehicle to draw a trailer or semi-trailer not owned by the permit holder, subject to conditions
e: Section 66: a goods carriage permit allows drawing trailers not owned by the holder; a stage carriage permit may conditionally allow use as a contract or goods carriage; s.83 permits replacement of vehicles.

t: Per Mukund Dewangan, the insertion of 'transport vehicle' in Form 4 of the CMV Rules in 1994 applies to:
o: Tractors and road rollers only
Only the categories substituted in 1994 – medium and heavy goods/passenger vehicles – and not to LMV-class transport vehicles
Two-wheelers used for delivery services
All vehicles used for hire or reward including motor cabs
e: The Court held that the procedure for an LMV licence was unchanged by the 1994 amendment; a separate transport endorsement is needed only for vehicles above 7,500 kg.

t: A Tribunal computes a 2024 death award using Sarla Verma's multiplier but adopts the Second Schedule structured formula amounts for conventional heads. This is:
o: Incorrect – conventional heads are not payable in s.166 claims
Incorrect – the Second Schedule/s.163A was deleted and conventional heads must follow Pranay Sethi (₹15,000/₹40,000/₹15,000 with 10% enhancement every three years)
Correct – the Second Schedule still governs conventional heads
Correct – Tribunals may choose whichever is higher
e: Section 163A with Schedule II was omitted in 2019; Pranay Sethi standardised conventional heads for s.166 claims with periodic 10% enhancement.

t: An employer's private car carries two employees to a site; the car overturns due to the driver's negligence and both employees are injured. The private car policy was issued in 2024. The insurer's liability for the employees is:
o: Covered – IMT-29 (legal liability to employees travelling in the employer's vehicle) is an inbuilt cover in private car TP sections from October 2023
Covered only under the compulsory PA cover
Covered only if ₹50 per employee was paid
Excluded, as employees are not third parties
e: From the IRDAI circular of 18.10.2023, IMT-29 is compulsory and inbuilt in private car package/bundled/stand-alone TP policies without additional premium.

t: The minimum paid-up equity capital required to start a life or general insurance company in India is:
o: ₹50 crore
₹100 crore
₹200 crore
₹500 crore
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). ₹100 crore for a direct insurer; ₹200 crore for a reinsurer (Section 6 of the Insurance Act).

t: Under the amended Section 194E, not giving way to an ambulance or other emergency vehicle attracts:
o: Community service only
Fine of ₹10,000 and/or imprisonment up to six months
Fine of ₹500
Fine of ₹1,000
e: Section 194E (new): fine ₹10,000 or imprisonment up to six months or both; it supports the golden-hour objective of the amendment.

t: A stage carriage with 40 registered seats is caught carrying 50 passengers. The fine under Section 194A is:
o: ₹500 per passenger
₹2,000 (₹200 per excess passenger)
e: Section 194A: ₹200 per excess passenger; 10 excess × ₹200 = ₹2,000, and the excess passengers must be off-loaded.

t: A 27-year-old permanent employee earning ₹40,000 per month dies leaving wife, one child and both parents. Loss of dependency is:
A 50-year-old self-employed trader earning ₹30,000 per month dies leaving a wife and two children. Loss of dependency is:
A 44-year-old employee on a fixed (non-permanent) salary of ₹24,000 per month dies in 2025 leaving wife, two children and both parents. Total compensation including conventional heads (+20%) is:
A 24-year-old self-employed tailor earning ₹15,000 per month loses his right hand (assessed 70% loss of earning capacity). Compensation for loss of future earnings, applying 40% future prospects, is:
e: 1,80,000 + 40% = 2,52,000 × 70% = 1,76,400 per annum × multiplier 18 (21–25) = ₹31,75,200; no personal-expense deduction in injury cases.

t: The control level of solvency ratio that every insurer must maintain is:
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). Available solvency margin must be at least 150% of the required solvency margin; falling below triggers IRDAI action.

t: On a contested award of ₹21,18,000, interest of ₹2,65,475 accrues and TDS of ₹26,547 is deducted. The total amount payable by the insurer, excluding costs, is:
e: Award 21,18,000 + net interest (2,65,475 − 26,547 = 2,38,928) = ₹23,56,928, plus costs as directed in the award.

t: An award of ₹25,00,000 carries 7.5% simple interest for 3 years, shared equally among five claimants, none of whom has furnished PAN. TDS deducted from each claimant's interest is:
o: Nil

t: The deceased in a 2025 accident leaves wife, one child and both parents. Loss of estate and funeral expenses together (with +20% enhancement) amount to:
e: Loss of estate 15,000 + 20% = 18,000 and funeral expenses 15,000 + 20% = 18,000 → ₹36,000, irrespective of the number of claimants (consortium is separate).

t: A self-employed deceased aged 39 earning ₹25,000 per month leaves wife, two children and mother. The monthly contribution to the family (after future prospects and deduction) is:
e: 25,000 + 40% = 35,000; four dependants → deduct 1/4 = ₹26,250 per month (annual multiplicand 3,15,000 × multiplier 15 = 47,25,000).

t: A hit-and-run victim with grievous hurt had earlier received ₹20,000 from a State relief fund for the same accident. The amount payable under Section 161 is:
e: Grievous hurt under s.161 is ₹50,000; any compensation received earlier for the same accident is adjusted: 50,000 − 20,000 = ₹30,000.

t: A 56-year-old permanent employee earning ₹50,000 per month dies leaving wife, two married sons and an unmarried daughter (four dependants claimed). Loss of dependency is:
e: 6,00,000 + 15% (permanent job, above 50) = 6,90,000; four dependants → deduct 1/4 = 5,17,500; × multiplier 9 (56–60) = ₹46,57,500.
